silo_relevance: This paper is highly relevant to derivative_pricing because it presents an end-to-end quantum workflow for loading terminal asset-price distributions and estimating expected option payoffs, including non-lognormal and real-market implied distributions. Its main value for this silo is the combination of distribution loading, option payoff estimation, and empirical tests on lognormal, Heston, digital, and real option data.

key_points.point: End-to-end quantum option-pricing pipeline with distribution loading and IQAE payoff estimation
key_points.silo_note: Directly targets derivative pricing by turning a terminal-price distribution into an expected option payoff estimate, which is the core computational task in pricing.

key_points.point: Supports pricing beyond the standard lognormal assumption, including Heston and real implied distributions
key_points.silo_note: Important for derivative_pricing because many products are priced off non-lognormal or market-implied terminal distributions rather than a simple benchmark model.

key_points.point: Wasserstein-trained hybrid qWGAN improves fit and therefore pricing accuracy versus BCE
key_points.silo_note: For derivative pricing, better distribution fit matters because payoff estimates depend on the loaded terminal distribution; the paper reports more accurate expected payoff estimates under the Wasserstein setup.

key_points.point: Digital payoff experiment shows the method remains accurate for non-smooth payoff structures
key_points.silo_note: This is especially relevant to derivative_pricing because digital options are a distinct payoff class and test whether the pricing workflow handles discontinuous payoffs well.

key_points.point: Practical limitations affect pricing deployment on current hardware
key_points.silo_note: For derivative_pricing, the main caveat is that real-hardware and real-data pricing are constrained by noise, training instability, and the fact that terminal distributions must be approximated from implied data.
